1044.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1044.hook: the Yoga Sutras open with atha, now, and the th in it isn't the th in think
1044.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1044.howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit learn each consonant in a plain and a breathed form, kha after ka and gha after ga, and practice them aloud, often holding a hand before the mouth to feel the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, the dot underneath: the tongue curled back, and the r that is a vowel, in Kṛṣṇa. Did you let your tongue curl back for it? Today, the letter h, and a lot of breath. Day one thousand forty-four.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali begin with a short word: atha. Now. Now, the teaching of yoga. An English reader sees t, h and says it the way you'd say thin, or this. Atha, with the tongue between the teeth. It's a natural guess. English has trained us to read t, h as one sound. But in Sanskrit, the h after a consonant isn't part of a new sound at all. It's breath. And once you hear that, a whole set of familiar words changes shape: Bhagavad, dharma, dhyana, bhakti. Today, the breath letters.
screen: `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING OF YOGA.` → `NOT THE TH IN THIN.` → `THE H IS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Go back to the map of the mouth. Each row runs in the same order: ka, kha, ga, gha, and the nasal. Look at the second and fourth sounds. They're the first and third with a puff of air added. That added h means: let breath out with it. So th is a t followed by a little breath, the way t and h meet in the English word hothouse, or a lighthouse. Atha is a-t-ha, the t at the teeth, then air. Ph is not f. It's a p with breath, as in uphill. Phala, fruit, is p-hala, not fala. Bh is a b with breath, as in clubhouse. That's the start of Bhagavad. Dh is a d with breath, as in roadhouse. That's dharma, and dhyana, meditation. The grammarians gave these sounds a pair of names. A plain consonant is alpaprana, little breath. One with the h is mahaprana, great breath. Prana: the same word this part of the year has used for the breath and the life in it. So the alphabet itself sorts its letters by how much breath each one carries. When you read a Sanskrit word, the h after a consonant is a small instruction to let the breath through. A reader who has practiced pranayama on this path already knows how to do that. Now it shows up inside the words. Bhagavad Gita doesn't start with a b. It starts with a b that breathes. And dharma, a word you've met many times on this path, opens with a d that lets out a little air before it says anything else.
screen: `EACH ROW: PLAIN, THEN WITH BREATH.` · `TH AS IN HOTHOUSE. PH AS IN UPHILL.` · `BH, CLUBHOUSE. DH, ROADHOUSE.` · `ALPAPRANA AND MAHAPRANA.` · then, large: `THE H IS BREATH.`

segments.voice: Hold your palm a few inches in front of your mouth. Say pa. Then pha, with breath, and feel the air land on your palm. Pa. Pha. Then ta and tha. Then ba and bha, and da and dha, letting the breath come through on the second of each pair. Go slowly, and notice how little effort it takes: just let the air out a moment longer. Then lower the hand and say one word, slowly, letting every breath letter breathe: dharma. Or Bhagavad. If you pray, you can say a name you pray with this way. If not, just feel the breath move. The bell holds the time.
Bha. A b with breath, the sound that opens Bhagavad. The breath letters: an h after a consonant means a puff of air, little breath and great breath.
Your line: let one of them breathe. Today, when you read a word with th, ph, bh or dh, let one of them breathe instead of turning it into an English sound. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1045.hook: a peace chant ends with shantih, and the h at the end is a breath that echoes the vowel before it
1045.carry: say saṃskṛta slowly, the way it's written
1045.tomorrow: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1045.howItsDone: Reciters close peace chants with om shantih shantih shantih, letting the final visarga breathe out softly, often with a faint echo of the vowel; the anusvara is sounded as a nasal hum, as in om.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, the breath letters: the h after a consonant is a puff of air. Atha, not the th in thin. Did you let one of them breathe? Today, the sounds that come after the vowel. Day one thousand forty-five.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE H IS BREATH.`

segments.voice: At the start of the Taittiriya Upanishad, a peace chant asks the gods to be gracious, and asks protection for the one who learns and the one who teaches. And it closes with these words: om, shantih, shantih, shantih. Peace, peace, peace. Listen to someone recite it, and the last word may sound a little longer than it's spelled. Shanti-hi. Where did that extra hi come from? It isn't added. It's written there, in a mark English letters barely show: one small h with a dot under it. Today, the two marks that live after a vowel.
screen: `OM, SHANTIH, SHANTIH, SHANTIH.` → `SHANTI-HI?` → `TWO MARKS AFTER A VOWEL.`

segments.voice: The first mark is called visarga. In Devanagari it looks like a colon after the letter, two small dots stacked. In transliteration, an h with a dot underneath. It's a release of breath after a vowel, and reciters often let that breath carry a faint echo of the vowel before it. So shantiḥ is heard as shanti-hi. Namaḥ, a bow, as in om namah shivaya, is heard as nama-ha when it stands alone. The echo is soft. It's the vowel's breath going out, not a new syllable shouted. Some teachers keep it barely audible; others let it ring. Both are heard. The second mark is anusvara: a single dot above the letter in Devanagari, and in transliteration an m with a dot, above or below. It's a hum after a vowel, a sound carried through the nose. One example is the sacred syllable itself, oṃ, which closes in that hum. And here's the detail to keep: the name of the language. In Sanskrit it's saṃskṛta. S-a, then an anusvara hum, then s-k, then the r-vowel from two days ago, then t-a. Sum-skri-tuh. The name you've been saying all week holds the dot above and the r that is a vowel. These two marks finish this week's tour of the marks. A vowel can be short or long. A consonant can be plain or breathed, at the teeth or curled back. And after the vowel, two last things can happen: the breath goes out, or the sound hums on. A reader who knows them can hear a chant end the way it was meant to end, with the peace still breathing after the word is over.
screen: `VISARGA: A BREATH AFTER THE VOWEL.` · `SHANTIH IS HEARD SHANTI-HI.` · `ANUSVARA: A HUM, AS IN OṂ.` · `SAṂSKṚTA: THE NAME ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE PEACE STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. On one out-breath, say softly: shantiḥ. Let the breath at the end carry the faint echo, shanti-hi, and fade. Breathe in. Do it again, quieter. Then switch to the hum: on the next out-breath, say oṃ, and let the m hum on through the nose until the breath runs out. Feel the difference. One sound opens and releases. The other closes and vibrates. Alternate slowly, one on each breath. If you'd rather not chant these words, hum without words, and then simply breathe out with an open mouth. The bell holds the time.
Visarga. The breath after the vowel, as in shantiḥ, said shanti-hi, and anusvara, the hum, as in oṃ.

Your line: say saṃskṛta slowly, the way it's written. Today, say the name of the language once, slowly, the way it's written: saṃskṛta, with the hum and the r-vowel inside it. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
1046.hook: one half-line of the Gita, read aloud with everything this week taught
1046.carry: do it carefully, piece by piece
1046.howItsDone: Students of the Gita often learn to recite verses in Sanskrit with a teacher, line by line, attending to vowel length, the place of each consonant, and the way words join.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, the two marks after a vowel: visarga, the breath, as in shantiḥ, and anusvara, the hum, as in oṃ. Did you say saṃskṛta slowly? Today, the last of these sounds, and one real line. Day one thousand forty-six.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE BREATH AND THE HUM.`

segments.voice: Here is a line from the second chapter of the Gita, in the careful English spelling: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana. A week ago, that string might have looked like a wall of letters with dots and dashes stuck to it. Today it's a set of instructions. Every mark on it is something this week taught. Its sense, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. So let's read it the way a reciter would, piece by piece.
screen: `KARMAṆY EVĀDHIKĀRAS TE.` → `MĀ PHALEṢU KADĀCANA.` → `A SET OF INSTRUCTIONS.`

segments.voice: Karmaṇy. The n has a dot under it: curl the tongue back. Karma-ny. Evādhikāras. This one is two words that ran together. Eva, alone, and adhikāraḥ, right. When one a meets another, they merge into a long ā, with the line over it. And the visarga at the end of adhikāraḥ has turned into an s, because a t comes next. That's the last item on the Upanishad's list from the start of the week: santana, the joining. In Sanskrit, words lean into each other, and the sounds change where they touch. Te: to you, a plain t at the teeth. Mā: long, a full open ah. Not. Phaleṣu: ph is a p with breath, never an f. Then the s with a dot, curled back. In the fruits. Kadācana: c is always ch, and the middle a is long. Ka-dah-chuh-nuh. Ever. Put together, slowly: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana. Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Now look at what the week gave. The plain a, inside almost every letter. The line that says stay longer. The map of the mouth, from throat to lips. The dot that curls the tongue. The h that is breath. The breath and the hum after a vowel. And now the joining. None of it is required to love this line. The Gita can be held close without reading a word of Sanskrit. But a reader who knows the sounds can hear the line as its reciters hear it. And there's a quiet fit in that. The line itself says the work is yours and the fruit isn't. Saying it carefully, sound by sound, is a small piece of that work, done for its own sake.
screen: `KARMAṆY: CURL FOR THE Ṇ.` · `EVA + ADHIKĀRAḤ: THE JOINING.` · `PHALEṢU: PH BREATHES, Ṣ CURLS.` · `KADĀCANA: C IS CH, Ā IS LONG.` · then, large: `THE WORK IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Say the first half slowly, one piece per breath. Karmaṇy, curling the tongue. Evādhikāras, holding the long ā. Te. Then the second half. Mā, long and open. Phaleṣu, letting the ph breathe. Kadācana, with the ch. Then say the whole line once, slowly, in one or two breaths. After that, stop speaking. Sit in the quiet the line leaves behind. If a result you're waiting on comes to mind, let it rest there, outside your hands, and come back to the breath. If speaking isn't possible, read the line inwardly. The bell holds the time.
Santana. The joining: words that lean into each other, read whole in one line of the Gita, karmaṇy evādhikāras te.

Your line: do it carefully, piece by piece. Today, do one task carefully for its own sake, the way you said that line, piece by piece, and leave the result where it belongs. Day one thousand forty-six.

1047.title: the summit sit
1047.hook: the Mahabharata nears its end on a mountain road, with a dog walking behind a king
1047.carry: stay beside it a little longer
1047.howItsDone: The Mahabharata lives in recitations, retellings, plays and television serials; the story of Yudhishthira refusing heaven without the dog is retold as a teaching about loyalty and dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the practices with Sanskrit sounds for readers, the alphabet heard before it is seen. Did you do one thing carefully, piece by piece? Today the last block of the year begins. Day one thousand forty-seven.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE ALPHABET, IN SOUND.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi leave their kingdom on foot. A dog falls in behind them and keeps walking. At last they turn north, toward the mountains. On the slope, one walker falls, then another, then another. Yudhishthira, the eldest, keeps going and does not look back. Only the dog is still beside him when a chariot comes down to meet him. This week opens the year's last block, and its days share one name: the summit sit. Each day climbs back to one stretch of the year and sits there. Today, the great story.
screen: `FIVE BROTHERS, DRAUPADI, AND A DOG.` → `ONE BY ONE, THEY FALL.` → `A WEEK OF SUMMIT SITS.`

segments.voice: The walk has a book of its own inside the epic, the Book of the Great Journey. As each walker falls, Bhima asks his brother why, and Yudhishthira names a cause: a pride, a partiality, an appetite, something each one carried the whole way up. He does not stop to mourn. He walks on. Then Indra, king of the gods, arrives in his chariot and invites Yudhishthira to rise to heaven in his own body. There is one condition. The dog stays behind. Yudhishthira refuses. In the story's words, paraphrased: to abandon one who is devoted to you, one who is frightened and has no other refuge, is a grave wrong, and he will not do it, not even for heaven. Indra argues. Yudhishthira holds. And then the dog changes form. It was Dharma himself, the god of righteousness, who in the story is Yudhishthira's own father, testing his son again, as he once did as the Yaksha at the lake. Now step back and see the whole story from up here. The snake sacrifice that frames it. Bhishma's vow. The dice game and Draupadi's question. The Yaksha at the lake. The battlefield and the Gita spoken on it. Gandhari's grief. A story that size could have closed on a war. Near its end it stops instead on a tired man who will not leave a dog on a mountain. Whatever else dharma means across all those books, this test of it is small, and personal, and costs a great deal.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE GREAT JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE, THE WALKERS FALL.` · `NOT WITHOUT THE DOG.` · `THE DOG WAS DHARMA.` · then, large: `A SMALL LOYALTY, AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably for the bell's two minutes. Let the great story walk past you, one figure at a time: Bhishma, Kunti, Karna, Draupadi, Arjuna, Gandhari, Yudhishthira. Don't hold on to any of them. Let each one go by. If one stays, notice who it is, and let that be all right. In the last breaths, bring to mind someone who has walked beside you through a hard stretch of your own road. Just their face. The bell holds the time.
Dharma. Right conduct, tested once more at the end of the great story, in a king who would not leave a dog on the mountain.

Your line: stay beside it a little longer. Today, notice one being that stays beside you without being asked: a friend, a coworker, an animal. Stay beside it a little longer than you need to. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: the summit sit
1048.hook: a mother looks into her small son's mouth for dirt and sees everything there is, herself included
1048.carry: come back to something small and near
1048.howItsDone: The story of Yashoda seeing the universe in Krishna's mouth is told and sung in homes and temples, painted in miniatures, and retold during Janmashtami; devotees speak of vatsalya, loving God as a parent loves a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit looked back at the great story and ended with a king who would not leave a dog on a mountain. Did you stay beside it a little longer? Today we climb back to a smaller house. Day one thousand forty-eight.

The other boys come running to Yashoda with a complaint: Krishna has been eating dirt. She grabs his hand and scolds him. He looks up, all innocence, and says they're lying. If she doesn't believe him, she can look for herself. So she does the obvious thing. She says, open your mouth. He opens it. And she does not find dirt. That scene, from the Bhagavata Purana, is where today's summit sit goes: back to the weeks of Krishna's childhood, and to the mother who saw too much.
screen: `HE'S BEEN EATING DIRT.` → `OPEN YOUR MOUTH.` → `NO DIRT.`

segments.voice: Here is what the Bhagavata says she saw, in paraphrase. Inside the little mouth: the sky in every direction, the mountains, the islands and the oceans, the earth, the wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The whole moving world. And then, inside all of that, the village of Vraja. And inside the village, herself, standing there, looking into a child's mouth. Yashoda is shaken. The text lets her wonder aloud: is this a dream? Is it a trick of the gods' illusion? Is it some power in my own boy? She bows, in her heart, to the one who holds all of it. And then comes the turn this summit sit came for. The text says Krishna spread his maya over her, his power of veiling, in the form of a mother's love. She forgets what she has seen. She lifts him onto her lap, and he is her son again, a boy who may or may not have eaten dirt. Look back across the Krishna weeks: the prison birth, the crossing of the Yamuna, Putana, the butter, Kaliya, the mountain lifted, the flute, the dance, the leaving. Again and again the stories hold the same two things at once. The child is the whole universe. The child is also just a child who needs his face washed. Yashoda is given the vast vision for a moment, and then given back the small one. In the text, the veil that makes her forget is woven of a mother's love. Some readers hear that as a gift, not a loss: the ordinary love handed back.
screen: `THE WHOLE WORLD IN A CHILD'S MOUTH.` · `AND HERSELF, INSIDE IT.` · `A DREAM, A TRICK, OR MY SON?` · `SHE FORGETS, AND HOLDS HIM.` · then, large: `VAST, AND SMALL, AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes, and let this be a sit in two halves. For the first half, widen. Let your attention open past the room, past the building, out to the sky and whatever is under it, as far as it will go. Don't strain. Just let it open. Then, halfway, come home. Let it settle on one small thing close by: your hands, the breath at your nose, a cup on the table. Stay there, with the small thing, as if it were enough. The bell holds the time.
Vatsalya. Tender parental love, the veil that let Yashoda hold her son again after she saw the whole universe in his mouth.

Your line: come back to something small and near. Today, when you catch yourself thinking about something huge, come back once to something small and near: a face, a meal, a hand to hold. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: the summit sit
1049.hook: a weaver, a tailor, a shopkeeper and a princess, all singing to God in the language of home
1049.carry: say one kind thing in your first language
1049.howItsDone: The songs of the bhakti saints are sung in homes, temples and on pilgrim walks across India: Tukaram's abhangas, Kabir's dohas, Mirabai's bhajans and Andal's Tiruppavai, each in its own language.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to Krishna's childhood, and Yashoda saw the universe and was given back her son. Did you come back to something small and near? Today, the singers. Day one thousand forty-nine.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `VAST, AND SMALL, AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: A weaver at his loom in Varanasi, throwing the shuttle and singing. A tailor in Maharashtra with a needle in his hand and a name of God on his lips. A shopkeeper whose ledgers of money owed to him, the story goes, ended up in the river. A princess in Rajasthan who sang that she had no one but Krishna. A girl in a Tamil temple town who wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered. Those are some of the faces from the weeks of the saints of bhakti. Today's summit sit climbs back to them.
screen: `A WEAVER, A TAILOR, A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A PRINCESS, A GARDEN GIRL.` → `THE SAINTS OF BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: From the top of the year, look at who the tradition chose to remember. Kabir is remembered as a weaver. Namdev as a tailor. Tukaram as a small trader whose business failed. Mirabai as a princess who walked away from palace rules. Andal as a girl raised by a temple gardener. Looms, needles, ledgers, a palace, a garden. They're remembered for what they sang. And notice what they sang in. Andal and the Nayanars sang in Tamil. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram in Marathi. Kabir, Surdas, Tulsidas and Mirabai in the spoken tongues of the north. In Bengal, the songs of Chaitanya's kirtan were made in Bengali. The language of the kitchen and the market became a language of prayer. Listen to the kind of thing they said. A song credited to Kabir lets God speak, in paraphrase: where are you looking for me? I am right beside you. Not in the temple, not in the mosque, not in ritual and renunciation. Seek truly and you will find me in a moment. Mirabai, in paraphrase: my own is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. Different saints, different gods named, different tongues. One shared move: love spoken plainly, by whoever you happen to be, wherever you happen to stand. Songs from those weeks are still sung by heart in kitchens, on pilgrim roads, and in temple halls.

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes. Find the language you first heard tenderness in, whatever it is. If you pray, you can let one name of God, in that language, rest on the breath, quietly, again and again, the way the saints repeated a name. If you don't, choose a plain word for thanks in that same tongue. No need to say it aloud. Let it come and go with the breath, like a weaver's shuttle, back and forth. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Loving devotion, the saints' whole path, sung to God in the language of home.

Your line: say one kind thing in your first language. Today, say one kind thing in the language you grew up with, to someone who will understand it, or quietly to yourself. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: the summit sit
1050.hook: a monk in Chicago opens with "Sisters and Brothers of America", and a quiet teacher on a hill asks one question
1050.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry by asking "who am I?" whenever thoughts arise, in sitting practice and in daily life; Vivekananda's addresses and Tagore's Gitanjali are read and recited widely.

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to the saints of bhakti, singing in the language of home. Did you say one kind thing in your first language? Today, the modern teachers. Day one thousand fifty.

"Sisters and Brothers of America." Five words, and a monk in an ochre robe has a hall in Chicago listening. That's how Swami Vivekananda began his address there. Far from any podium, on a hill in south India, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi was giving people a question small enough to carry in a pocket. Between those two rooms sit the weeks of the modern teachers: Ramakrishna, Vivekananda, Ramana, Aurobindo, Gandhi, Tagore. Today's summit sit climbs back to them, and sits with the pocket question.
screen: `SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA.` → `A HALL, AND A HILL.` → `THE MODERN TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Look back at that block from up here. Ramakrishna, a temple priest whose sayings his followers wrote down. Vivekananda, carrying Vedanta and yoga to lecture halls abroad. Aurobindo writing about the divine at work in ordinary life. Gandhi reading the Gita as a handbook for action without clinging to results. Tagore turning prayer into short poems in Gitanjali. Very different people. And then Ramana, whose central teaching fits in three words: who am I? Here is how the short text called Who Am I? works it, in paraphrase. Thoughts will keep arising. Don't chase them and don't fight them. When one comes, ask: to whom has this thought come? The answer will be: to me. Then ask: who am I? Ramana says the mind then turns back toward its source, and the thought that rose falls quiet. Do this each time, and the questioning itself, he says, wears the other thoughts away, the way a stick used to stir a funeral fire is burned up in the end. That's an unusual picture to leave people with. The question is not a puzzle to solve with a clever answer. Ramana is clear that an answer like "I am this body" doesn't finish it. The question is a tool for turning attention around, from the things that appear to the one they appear to. Across all six teachers, something like that keeps happening: an ancient path, carried into a modern room, made small enough for one person to use.
screen: `SIX TEACHERS, SIX ROOMS.` · `TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME?` · `TO ME. THEN, WHO AM I?` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.` · then, large: `TURN ATTENTION AROUND.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes, and let the breath settle. Thoughts will come. That's fine. When one arrives, don't follow it and don't push it away. Ask, quietly: to whom did this come? The answer: to me. Then ask: who am I? Don't answer in words. Just let attention turn back toward the one who is asking, and rest there until the next thought comes. Then the question again. The bell holds the time.
Ramana. The teacher whose whole path fits in one question: who am I?
Your line: to whom did this come? Today, when a worry shows up, ask it once: to whom did you come? And notice who answers. Day one thousand fifty.
